notable_claims: Personal non-commercial computer use should be tolerated if it does not substantially increase costs.
Universities and Congress should establish a legal right to the privacy of email.
Universities should tolerate hypothetical legal risks associated with user postings on email or Usenet.
Computers provide an opportunity to extend freedom of the press beyond print media due to low distribution costs.
classification.summary: John McCarthy outlines proposed policies for universities regarding computer use. He advocates for the tolerance of personal non-commercial use, the establishment of email privacy rights, and the protection of electronic speech on Usenet and mailing lists.
classification.title: Computers and Academic Freedom mailing list (batch edition)

identity.subject: Computers and Academic Freedom mailing list (batch edition)

notable_claims: NCSA policy granted the director the right to monitor email
Warning users of potential monitoring is insufficient justification for doing so
classification.summary: The author critiques the National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) policy that grants its director the right to monitor employee email. The post argues that simply warning users that mail may be opened does not justify the act of opening it. It notes that while NCSA sought suggestions for revising the policy, no actual suspension of monitoring rights had occurred.
classification.title: Re: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom

identity.subject: Re: New NCSA e-mail policy inconsistent with Academic Freedom

notable_claims: Information in a user's disk files is private even if the user does not own the disk.
Computer and network access should not be denied without due process.
Warrants must be obtained prior to searches of computer systems.
Resource limitations should be managed via quotas rather than restrictions on how resources are used.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie proposes a framework for academic freedoms as applied to computer use. He categorizes these rights into freedom of expression, privacy, due process, access, and resource limits. The proposal emphasizes that users should own the information in their files regardless of hardware ownership.
classification.title: Which rights?

notable_claims: Privacy rights for electronic documents should mirror the protections afforded to physical offices and desks.
Members of a university community do not surrender their constitutional rights of privacy by joining the academic community.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that privacy rights for electronic files should be analogous to the privacy of physical desks and offices. He cites university student codes and ACLU guidance on Fourth Amendment rights to argue against the notion that working at a public university eliminates an individual's right to privacy.
classification.title: RE: Which rights?

notable_claims: Institutions use waivers to justify searching user files without cause or terminating accounts without notice.
Students should have clearly defined means to participate in the formulation of institutional policy.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie discusses the necessity of an appeals process for institutional rules and argues that students and faculty should participate in policy formulation. He specifically criticizes the practice of requiring users to sign waivers granting institutions unrestricted access to their computer files as a condition for obtaining an account.
classification.title: Which Rights?

notable_claims: Newsgroups are functionally equivalent to serials/periodicals and thus covered by library policies.
Some electronic journals on Usenet have been assigned ISSN numbers.
sci.psychology.digest was recognized as one of the best new magazines of 1990 by Library Journal.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie argues that Usenet newsgroups should be classified as serials or periodicals rather than mere communication tools. He contends that this classification brings them under the protection of existing library policies, specifically citing the American Library Association's Freedom To Read statement.
classification.title: Re: Which Rights?

notable_claims: The NCSA revised its email policy on April 23, 1991, after a critique claimed it was inconsistent with the Constitution and academic freedom.
Stanford University suppressed 'rec.humor.funny' in 1989 but re-installed it following a campaign.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie announces that back issues of CAF-news and a collection of university computer policy statements are available via anonymous FTP from eff.org. The archive includes materials on email privacy, the Electronic Communications Privacy Act of 1986, and documentation regarding censorship efforts at Stanford University and the NCSA.
classification.title: New to the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) archive

identity.subject: New to the Computers and Academic Freedom (CAF) archive

notable_claims: University computing policies are often heavy on prohibitions and light on permissions.
Institutional policy typically evolves from informal to proscriptive, then toward a balance of rights and responsibilities.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie argues that university computing policies typically evolve from no policy to overly proscriptive regulations, and finally to a balance of rights and responsibilities. To illustrate this pattern, he provides a detailed historical case study of student policy evolution at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign from 1904 to 1973. He suggests that understanding this general institutional trajectory can help guide the development of academic computer policies.
classification.title: From Regulations to Rights: The Maturation of Policy

identity.subject: From Regulations to Rights: The Maturation of Policy

notable_claims: The BU IT policy allows the university to inspect any data or file without notice.
The policy prohibits making 'offensive or annoying material' accessible.
The policy allows for amendments at any time without prior notice.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques the Boston University Information Technology ethics policy of March 26, 1990. He argues that the policy's terms regarding data inspection and restrictions on 'offensive or annoying material' violate privacy and free speech. Kadie highlights the danger of applying restrictive computing policies to general campus life.
classification.title: Re: Harrassment via email

notable_claims: The OCF aims to ensure no member of the Berkeley campus community is denied sought computer resources.
No small number of people should control the accessibility of OCF sponsored computing facilities.
All official OCF documents must be provided to interested parties without undue delay.
classification.summary: This item provides the full text of the Constitution for Berkeley's Open Computing Facility (OCF), an organization dedicated to democratically managing open computing resources. The document outlines a governance structure involving active membership, elected officers, and faculty sponsors to ensure broad access to computer resources on campus. It includes a Bill of Rights covering nondiscrimination, privacy, and freedom of information.
classification.title: The OCF Constitution

identity.subject: Re: Need info on computer acct policy

notable_claims: System administrators should not intervene in irresponsible user behavior regarding disk space.
Resource allocation issues are best solved via departmental billing or increasing hardware capacity.
classification.summary: Joe Buck responds to a query regarding how system administrators should handle users who consume excessive disk quotas for email instead of research. Buck argues that administrators should not micromanage user behavior and suggests that resource shortages be solved through departmental billing or purchasing more hardware.
classification.title: Re: Email privacy vs. System management

identity.subject: Re: Email privacy vs. System management
